draft.title: Rivers and wetlands as environments
card: a channel of flowing fresh water that drains the land and carries water towards a lake or the sea.
low land that is covered by shallow water for part or all of the year, such as a marsh or a billabong.
Rivers and wetlands hold water and filter it. Plants and soil trap sediment and some pollutants, so the water that moves on is cleaner.
Wetlands soak up floodwater and release it slowly, which helps prevent floods. They also give homes to fish, birds and plants. Many native species need natural floods to breed.
draft.remember: Rivers and wetlands store and filter water, help prevent floods and are homes for wildlife that often rely on natural floods.

a.q: A wetland lies beside a town in Victoria. After heavy rain it fills with water and then drains slowly. Which role of the wetland does this show?
opts: It helps prevent floods
It filters pollutants from water
It gives birds a place to nest
It helps fish breed after floods
a.why: Soaking up floodwater and releasing it slowly reduces the water that reaches the town at once, so it helps prevent floods. Filtering is a different role, because it is about cleaning the water, not about how fast the water moves.
a.clue: Think about what happens to the speed and amount of water moving on.

b.q: A native fish in a river needs a natural flood to trigger breeding. A dam now holds back flood flows. What is the most likely effect on the fish?
opts: Fewer fish may breed successfully
The fish breed more often than before
The fish no longer need water to breed
The fish breed in the dam instead
b.why: The card says many native species need natural floods to breed. If floods are held back, these fish may breed less successfully. The fish do not simply switch to breeding more often, because their breeding relies on the flood.
b.clue: What does this fish need in order to breed?

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('may'), and the distractors are implausible ('no longer need water to breed', 'breed in the dam instead'). A student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.

The scenario turns on a dam holding back flood flows. Dams changing natural flows belong to point 2 (causes of river decline), and the effect on wildlife belongs to point 3. The question could test flood-triggered breeding without a dam, for example by using a dry year with no flood.

b.q: Native waterbirds at a wetland in northern Victoria rely on natural floods to breed. This year is dry, and no flood reaches the wetland. What is most likely to happen?
opts: Fewer waterbirds breed, as there is no flood
More waterbirds breed, as dry ground is safer for nests
Breeding rises, as no flood washes the nests away
Breeding is unchanged, as it follows the seasons
b.why: Many native species need natural floods to breed, so in a year with no flood, fewer of these waterbirds breed. Breeding does not simply stay the same with the seasons, because for these birds the flood, not the time of year, is what they need to breed.
b.clue: What do these birds need before they breed?

b.best: Fewer waterbirds breed, as there is no flood
